title: Introduction to LLM evaluations in 10 key ideas

segments.text:
[Music] Hi and welcome to the course on LLM 
evaluations. In this video, we're going to

talk about what LLM evaluations are and when you 
need them in 10 key ideas. This will be the one

theoretical video in this course, everything 
else will be hands-on. Now, LLM evaluations is

the process of assessing whether your AI system 
works well. Which brings us to the first point:

evaluating LLM systems is not the same as 
evaluating LLM models, which is usually done

through benchmarks. But these public benchmarks 
help you figure out, for example, which model is

better in coding and mathematics. But they are 
like school exams: they test general skills. And

if you're building a specific application like a 
chatbot or even a simpler prompt chain you need to

test it on the tasks that it is meant to solve. 
And it will consist not just from the model,

but the prompts, the application logic and 
everything else that you add on top of it.

So if you are building a RAG system don't search 
for a RAG benchmark - build your own. That's what

we're going to talk about in the course. One 
more thing to be clear: evaluations is not some

standalone activity like "doing evals". It is 
a tool that helps you answer questions and make

decisions about your product. And depending where 
you are in your product life cycle it can fit

into different workflows. If you're just building 
your product, it is often about experiments. Maybe

you're comparing different models or different 
prompts or you're trying to fix a particular

error mode that you observed. Evaluations help you 
objectively decide, for example, which prompt is

better: prompt A or prompt B. You can also run 
stress-testing or red-teaming where you send

tricky or adversarial inputs to your system to 
see if you can provoke it to do something unsafe.

For example, what if you ask your chatbot to do 
something inappropriate? Will it comply or not?

Once the system is in production, it is all about 
monitoring: you want to make sure that your users

are getting good experience. Like are they getting 
stuck? are there hallucinations? does the chatbot

deny to respond any questions that it should 
not? So you need continuous online evaluations.

And finally, there is regression testing. 
If you change something like fix a prompt,

try to fix a bug - before you roll out these 
changes you need to make sure that they don't

break anything else. So you need regression 
testing. In each of these cases evaluations

will look slightly differently. And they will 
evolve with your product, just like your product

itself. If you are coming from software background 
some of these things can sound very familiar,

like regression testing. However dealing with LLMs 
brings a whole new set of issues. Yes, you still

need to test your software, but now you also need 
to evaluation the contents of your interactions:

the inputs and outputs that your system gets. And 
that's quite different. First of all, LLMs are

non-deterministic which means that even for the 
exact same input you can get different outputs,

and that's sort of okay. You're also dealing 
with prompts which are very brittle. Sometimes

changing something very small like punctuation can 
actually alter the behavior of the system. You're

also often solving very open-ended tasks like for 
example generating emails. How do you even define

what a good email is? There are many answers 
to that. And finally because you're working

with probabilistic systems that generate language, 
you also now face new risks like hallucinations:

the model can make things up. Jailbreaks: users 
can try bypass the safety measures. Or data leaks

where LLMs can expose sensitive data. So with 
LLMs it's not enough to just test functionality,

you also need a way to evaluate the safety and 
quality of responses. The first obvious solution

to this complexity is manual evaluations, and 
honestly that's where you should start. You should

read the outputs you get, and this will help you 
build intuition, spot patterns and also understand

what "good" means in your use case. If you can 
ask subject matter experts to label some data,

this is priceless, especially early on. 
However, this doesn't scale. You cannot

continue manually labeling everything forever, so 
you need automations. And here is one important

point I want to make. Automated evaluations are 
there to scale your judgment, not to replace

it. If you don't know yet what you're evaluating 
manually, there is nothing to automate. You first

need to figure it out. But once you do, you can 
build very useful proxy metrics and signals both

for experiments and for production monitoring. 
You should still continue looking at the logs:

manual evaluations and automated evaluations 
go hand in hand. One will inform another. Now,

let's talk about the "how" of evaluations. There 
are two main types here. At a very high level,

the anatomy of a single eval is simple. You get 
an input, you run it through your application,

you capture the output and you evaluate it. 
But here is one difference: you can also add

a reference answer in the mix. So if you have 
this reference answer or so-called ground truth

response, you can run reference-based evaluations. 
There, the goal is to compare the answers you get

against some expected answers. So for example 
if you have a chatbot you can design a set of

test questions and expected answers to these 
questions and then evaluate if your system is

actually getting them correct. This is useful for 
regression testing and for experiments. And then

the second way to run evaluations is open-ended 
or reference-free evaluations. That's where

you don't have a correct answer in advance. For 
example, this applies to monitoring in production

or to very complex open-ended or conversational 
scenarios where it's difficult to come up with an

ideal response. In this case, you might measure 
the specific qualities of the outputs you get.

For example, its safety, politeness, correctness, 
length and so on. In both cases, we are talking

about datasets - and this is another important 
point. With LLMs you cannot just test that 2 plus

2 equals 4 and call it a day. You actually need 
to run evaluations across a range of possible

outputs. Which also means that you need to prepare 
them: so you need to design a test dataset that

represents your use case. You can actually have 
several datasets, for example, one will include

so-called "happy path" queries, so some expected 
normal inputs, another one would have some edge

cases which are important to you and you need to 
make sure that you get them right. and you can

also have some sort of adversarial dataset which 
will test your system for potential weak spots.

You can design these test cases manually or source 
them from real logs or some past history or even

generate synthetically, but you need to invest in 
actually designing that. When it comes to methods,

there are quite a few options out there: from 
deterministic ones like verifying that the code

that was generated by the LLM can actually run to 
machine learning based evaluations. But one of the

most popular methods that I want to highlight is 
called LLM as a judge. The idea is very simple:

you take the output that was generated by your 
system and you pass it to another LLM - or to

the same LLM for this matter - but with 
an evaluation prompt. Inside this prompt

you ask an LLM to assess a specific quality 
of the response or to grade it. For example,

"is this response based on the retrieved context"? 
or "does this response follow expected brand

guideline?" and so on. Effectively, you're using 
an LLM to replace a human labeler for a specific

narrow constrained task. And it works surprisingly 
well. Just remember that your LLM judge is like a

small machine learning project in itself and 
it also requires some tuning and evaluation.

we will have a separate session about that. One 
of the reasons why LLM judges are so popular is

because they let you implement custom criteria. 
and this is a core idea in LLM evaluations. You

actually need to figure out these criteria, 
not just pick some random metrics. Of course,

not all metrics are bad. If you're evaluating 
something objective like classification quality

or ranking quality, there are established metrics 
like precision, recall, NDCG and so on. But here

I'm talking about subjective qualities. You 
cannot just steal someone else's criteria

and expect to apply them to your product. You 
can of course borrow implementations. Like for

example if detecting personal data in outputs is 
important to you, you can reuse a PII detector.

But you cannot just apply the criteria from 
some other project to your project. You need

to figure out what matters in your use case. For 
example, take a criteria like "coherence". Most

modern LLMs can already generate very fluent and 
coherent output there is no point in measuring it:

you will just always pass. However if you're 
working with smaller LLMs or self-hosting small

open source models you might actually want to test 
for it, if this is the problem that you observe

in the outputs. Or take another example: OpenAI 
recently published one of their model cards and

there they share a specific test that they use for 
the model to make sure that it follows negative

instructions. Like for example: "don't contact 
customer support". Clearly, the need for this

test comes from a specific failure mode that they 
observed so they implemented a way to evaluate

for it. Would this apply to your product? Maybe. 
Maybe not. But this is a good example of how you

can implement evaluations which are informed by 
observing specific errors in production. By now,

you probably figured out that LLM evaluations are 
not just engineering. You start with qualitative

analysis and then you turn it quantitative. In 
fact, it's probably closer to product analytics

than it is to software observability. In software, 
you usually have an initial set of metrics to

start with, like latency and memory usage and 
so on. So you don't have to think too much about

that. But with LLM evaluations you first need 
to figure out what you're actually measuring. So

you need to look at the data and understand what 
type of behaviors you want to detect, what type of

errors you see and then figure out how you can 
design experiments around that. And to enable this

you also need logging. This is very important, 
you need to capture all the inputs and outputs.

You get you may first start with synthetic data 
but once you have real users you need to capture

everything to make use of this data in your 
evaluations and your product improvements. If

it sounds like building a solid evaluation system 
takes time - well it's because it does. But it's

time well spent. A good evaluation system is 
actually a competitive advantage. It is like a

living product spec which implements what "good" 
is for your use case in code and datasets. And

this lets you do a lot of great things. First of 
all, you can move faster: you can run experiments,

you can compare different prompts, you can test 
new models as they come out in hours not days.

Second, you can ship with confidence: you'll 
know if something will be broken after you make

a change. And lastly it helps you build trust with 
your users especially if you're operating in high

stakes and high-risk domains. This also creates a 
continuous improvement loop where every stage from

early experiments to live monitoring helps you get 
better. For example, as you learn from real users,

you can expand your tests with new edge 
cases and over time this can become a moat.

Everyone has access to the same models, but 
you can have access to good labeled data,

sharp tests which actually help you discriminate 
between good and bad, and product insights that

not everyone has. Okay, I know it was a lot 
of theory. But I hope I convinced you why

evaluations matter. Without evaluations, your 
product is just a prototype. And if you want to

dig into any of these ideas, we have a separate 
YouTube playlist with introduction to the evals.

In the following videos, we will get hands-on 
and we will start with implementing different

LLM evaluations methods on the toy dataset and 
see how it works. See you in the next videos!
